utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Dr. Donia is to return. My note is that he is to be recalled for 45 minutes cross-examination, and meanwhile, he is to review, or was to review the transcript of the 30th Session Minutes, 9th of May, 1993, at which Mr. Milosevic spoke. So what would seem to be sensible is that I will ask him first if there is anything he wants to add about that and then we will hear the cross-examination. And that is followed by -- if I'm right, by Witness B-1097, who was being cross-examined when the accused fell ill. My note is that there was half an hour, in that case, left of cross-examination when the witness returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That agrees with our records as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything anyone wants to add before we have Dr. Donia in? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only to say that perhaps after the second witness if I could address you on one or two procedural matters I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with the witnesses and then we'll hear those procedural matters. I should say, though, there is a change of dates which I can deal with now while it's in my mind and that is that the United Nations has changed the date of the Eid Al-Fitr holiday. As you know from the -- we have the dates here. It was on Tuesday the 25th. The date has been changed to Wednesday, the 26th. Sorry. It was -- I thank Judge Kwon. It was Wednesday the 26th; it is now the 25th. I take it that there is no objection to our changing those dates for the sitting, and we will now sit on Wednesday the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Donia, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, you are under the same declaration. There's no need to take it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for returning, first. You have been recalled. You were, I think, going to review the transcript of the 30th Session of the 9th of May, 1993, at which the accused spoke, and then there was also the matter of further cross-examination. Before the cross-examination, is there anything you want to add to what you said on the last occasion, anything about this particular transcript that you want to add, or we'll go straight into the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are a number of things about that transcript that I'd like to point out that came up in the prior questions, but I wonder if they may be covered in either cross-examination or redirect. However you would like me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with it this way, shall we: Let's hear the examination and the redirect. If there's anything at the end of it which you would like to add, of course you will have the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You have three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, in November 2001, you gave an interview to the paper Dani, and my question has to do with one of your responses to the question that was asked of you. They said you were a Hague witness twice, one of -- in Blaskic and the second time you went into the background of the conflict, and you were asked what your experience was with The Hague Tribunal. And the point of my question is the following: You go on to answer and say that: "Tadic is the most important case for me on the basis of which on the 15th of July, 1999, the basic fact was confirmed of the investigation and established that the activities of Serbia or, rather, Yugoslavia was an international armed conflict." So for you, Tadic is the most important case, where it was establish that what was happening in Yugoslavia at the time was an international armed conflict. Now, you as an historian, do you really and truly consider that what was going on within Yugoslavia was caused by the forceful secession of an international armed conflict, the forcible secession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I interrupt. This is really for the Court to determine. That should be said first. But the witness can, of course, answer as to his interview. And perhaps the best way to deal with it, to say, if you would, Dr. Donia, first of all whether what's been put to you is direct, that that is what you said, and then perhaps you'd like to amplify and clarify what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think I did indeed give an interview, and the essence of at least part of it was just conveyed by Mr. Milosevic. At that time, the Appeals Chamber decision in the Tadic case was relatively recent, and I viewed that as probably the most important conclusion to have come out of the Tribunal and accepted and accept its conclusions, again as an historian and not rendering a legal opinion, but that was my conclusion at the time and would still be the case, that that was an important step and one with which raw judgement I concur from a historical standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I'm asking you as an historian precisely. Don't you feel that historical facts are being restructured here, for example, in the Tadic case? And I don't think that anybody knows about him in Yugoslavia, that the facts are being established by way of the fact that Serbia and Yugoslavia was involved in an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Donia, do you know that this conflict emerged through the armed secession -- was caused by the armed secession of certain parts of what was once Yugoslavia and that it took place exclusively within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this conflict was caused by a determination on the part of you and others in the Belgrade leadership to prevent the peaceful secession of those republics from Yugoslavia as independent countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of the fact that it was precisely Yugoslavia which advocated a peaceful solution and even all the international mediators are well aware of that fact? Do you yourself know that it was precisely the activities of external factors, the premature recognition and pushing individual parts of Yugoslavia into a conflict amongst themselves caused the conflict and that the war was imposed upon Serbia? Do you know anything about that, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the principal cause was the determination of yourself and others in the Belgrade leadership to instigate uprisings amongst Serbs in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the peaceful process that was going forward, which was, for example, peaceful in the Soviet Union for almost all republics as that federation dissolved in the course of 1990 and 1991. So I cannot accept your premise. I disagree with your fundamental rendering of those -- those causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There'll be time to go into those causes in greater detail in due course in other areas, but you as an expert witness, as an historian yourself, deal here with the various Assembly sessions of Republika Srpska. Tell me, please, Mr. Donia, how many Assembly sessions did you deal with of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly certain. The total number of sessions was, I believe, 62, and in this report I've not dealt with the first 15 and dealt selectively with almost all of them after that. There were a few for which I did not have the complete transcript, and there were a few which had, in my view, nothing that rose to the standard that I was asked to examine these transcripts for. So I guess the answer probably is I deal with here about 35 or 40 sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you chose the sessions selectively, ones where you could pull out of context somebody's observations or conclusions. Is that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's wrong. I reviewed the transcripts and minutes with an eye toward selecting those citations which rose to the level of the things that I was asked to address, which were, first of all the fundamental policies of the Bosnian Serb leadership and then the relationship of that leadership to external factors, including international negotiators, yourself and the Belgrade leadership, Montenegrin leadership, paramilitaries, JNA, and other external factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that from the aspects of historical signs and your expertise that it is proper to extract several quotations from a particular Assembly session out of context and then, on the basis of that, to reconstruct some sort of headings or titles under which you accuse the Serb side of being responsible for the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you have mischaracterised both my intention and the outcome as you see it in the report. This was an examination in which the first thing I did in each Assembly session was to outline the context. There was a deliberate, conscious effort on my part to explain the context in which the debates and the citations took place. I had no intention of blaming what you call the Serb side. I was looking for evidence of the policies of the Bosnian Serb leadership as represented by the SDS and also its relationship to external factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, was it your task to take a look at the documents of the other two sides as well? And they had their organs, their assemblies, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to be more precise, when we had a member, Kljuic, here testifying, a member of the Bosnian state Presidency, I showed him the stenogram of a session he attended from which it could be seen that the Presidency, led by Izetbegovic, was fully aware of the unlawful mass confinement of Serbs in their camps, and so on and so forth. So these flagrant matters, did you analyse those when it comes to the Muslim side, for example?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions within that locution. My sole task for this particular case was to look at the Bosnian Serb Assembly minutes in the period beginning with the 16th Session. I did not look at any other Assembly sessions in connection with this task. I have looked at other minutes, meetings, press reports in conjunction with other sides, both for other cases in my preparation for those cases and in my own research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't deal with the other parties, other sides. Is that it, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report that you have before you and my summaries of it, I have dealt only with the Bosnian Serb Assembly, but as I said, I've reviewed other documents and reports for other situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since we have very little time, the way you portray things, let's take a look at the 33rd Session, for example, Assembly session, and you say - and I think that's on page 226, the ERN number and the last digits of that - where you say: "The Defence Ministry is currently negotiating the financing of all production of ammunition and equipment in the republic, and by means of compensatory agreements from the SRY and selling of goods from the war reserves," et cetera, et cetera. And you quote Krajisnik in that regard. Isn't it quite clear that the Ministry of Defence of the republic, or Republika Srpska -- or, rather, that Republika Srpska, let me put it that way, is negotiating with various enterprises in the FRY for the purchase of necessary goods?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've just not been able to -- could you give me your page reference again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is the 33rd Assembly session. The page in Serbian is 5526, the last digits. And after that, we come to Srebrenica and Zepa, and the title is "Srebrenica and Zepa Are Part of the RS."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can be of assistance. It's page 32 of Dr. Donia's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have it, Mr. Milosevic. I'm sorry, could I ask you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska is negotiating with different enterprises from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Well, you've had different texts from the purchase from abroad of necessary equipment and so on. So what is there that is out of ordinary, unusual there, or not normal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of those citations which speaks to the relationship between the Bosnian Serb leadership and an external entity, in this case the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or enterprises in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the sale of goods from war booty and commercial reserves. It therefore is included in the report as part of the effort to describe those -- capture what this source says about those relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you find in any of those texts that they weren't purchasing goods from enterprises in Yugoslavia alone but from other countries as well? Just give me a yes or no answer and we can move on, not to lose time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing any reference to purchases of munitions and equipment from other countries. I don't recall, or could potentially have been but I don't recall seeing any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to show you those quotations and look through all of them, but do you have any knowledge about the fact and did you have any dealings with the fact of where the Muslim side was getting assistance and weapons and munitions and everything else that Mr. Izetbegovic speaks about quite publicly about procuring? He said this in a public speech. He mentioned the figure of 300.000 weapons, millions of pieces of ammunition, and so on and so forth. So do you have any knowledge anywhere as to the sources of their equipment and goods?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is outside the realm of my brief for this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it was your brief merely to establish whether and to what extent the organs of Republika Srpska had any kind of - how shall I put this? - incriminatory acts that they could be accused of. So that is your task as an historian, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to describe, to capture as I was able through those citations, the relationship of the Bosnian Serb leadership, namely the key leaders of the SDS, with other external entities. Whether that is incriminating or is good or bad, or whatever it is, is not for me really to judge. That's something that is put forward here as part of the effort to characterise those relationships as seen through the eyes of the Bosnian Serb leaders themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that Assembly of Republika Srpska, the one you're analysing, was composed of people's deputies elected at direct multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war broke out and that it was a legitimate, lawful organ of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies who made up the Assembly of the Bosnian Serb Republic, or Republika Srpska, were elected in 1990 not as delegates to the Bosnian Serb Assembly but as delegates to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were elected from districts all over Bosnia-Herzegovina that had mixed populations and were specifically elected for the purpose of serving in the Assembly. That seems to me to raise a question of whether their break-away and formation was in fact a legal and fully warranted act in light of the fact that they formed a self-proclaimed body that had no constitutional status in the original documents under which they were elected. I, however, can't make that judgement. I'm not too sure that -- well, I'm certainly not a legal historian of the former Yugoslavia and would certainly defer to others to make that judgement, but it does seem to me that it's an open question as to their ability to represent the constituents which elected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Donia, that they represented the constituency that elected them, to use your words, only after the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, contrary to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and by ignoring the positions of representatives of the Serb people in that Assembly, took the decision on the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on? So the principle of consensus was not respected. What other choice did they have then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegates who made up the Bosnian Serb Assembly served in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think without exception from its convening in, I believe, December -- mid-December 1990 through 1992. In other words, at times when they were also serving as members of the self-proclaimed Bosnian -- Serbian -- or Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there was a period in which there was simultaneous representation, at least by a few people, in both Assemblies, and certainly the first thing that these delegates did was to serve in the body to which they were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They performed their duties in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they advocated a peaceful solution, as you know full well, and even with the help of the Carrington conference or, rather, his assistant, Ambassador Cutileiro, the three sides reached agreement over the so-called Carrington-Cutileiro plan signed by all three parties, and then Izetbegovic withdrew his signature upon instructions from your own ambassador and provoked a conflict. Are you aware of that as an historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I'm sure you're aware, Mr. Milosevic, the notion that that decision of Izetbegovic's was motivated by Mr. Zimmerman has been specifically denied by him publicly on numerous occasions, and I believe him. The question of the Cutileiro agreement, of course, is one that is beyond my specific competence here to address, and I would only note that it was one of many situations that arose in which the three sides were very close to agreement. If you'll recall, the Cutileiro agreement was an agreement in principle and not in details, with further specifics to be worked out. And owing to developments that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those further agreements on detail were never reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Without going into why something happened, let us go back within the framework of your expertise here. You refer to the 33rd Session, and your heading is "Srebrenica and Zepa are Part of Republika Srpska." Radovan Karadzic, at the 33rd Session, held on the 20th and 21st of July, 1993, spoke about Resolution 836 of the UN Security Council; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is part of his statement on the page we just quoted, and you put that under the heading of "Srebrenica and Zepa are Part of Republika Srpska" as being an allegation made by Karadzic. Is that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it, however, true that Karadzic speaks about the failure of the Resolution to be in conformity with the Geneva Conventions, which says that only demilitarised areas may be protected? That is what he speaks about, as far as I am able to read your own excerpts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth to last line in that citation begins - I'm citing the English here: "That's RS territory. That Muslim state has no right nor does it need to be a party to that agreement." That was the basis of the headline that I chose for that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's taken out of context, because he says in that same sentence: "Our Assembly must decide on any exception, for our Assembly enacted a general decision that UN forces not be deployed on our territory." Yet they were deployed there, and they were in both Srebrenica and Zepa. Is it true that Karadzic says that the demilitarisation of these two enclaves was not carried out and that only a small quantity of weapons had been surrendered? So the topic of discussion is a different one.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topics of discussion in this citation are actually several and all pertaining to Gorazde and Zepa, and in fact, Srebrenica, beginning with the discussion of the Resolution and the subsequent agreement that was reached on the ground and the fact, which is indeed the case, that the Assembly had adopted a general decision that UN forces not be deployed, and in other citations which I believe are included, had made exceptions for first the Canadian force that went into Srebrenica in April of 1993 and subsequently a unit of Ukrainians that was deployed, and later the exchange of forces of the Canadian for the Dutch forces. All that is consistent with his statement here and consistent with the statement that he made that in his view, these are part of RS territory, that's RS territory, and that the Muslim state has no right. So the headline in this case, I would argue, accurately reflects one part of what is covered here and captures an important part of what Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it contradictory that he speaks of exceptions and that it is through the agreement of the bodies of Republika Srpska that UN forces were deployed in Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's perfectly consistent. He's saying, "Our Assembly must decide on any exception." It subsequently did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They decided that those forces be deployed in Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. Wasn't that so, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to hear. And is it true that Republika Srpska never for a moment required that the Muslims hand over their weapons to them but exclusively to UN forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Karadzic's position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that same session in 1993, Karadzic speaks of Srebrenica as well, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Karadzic then said that if the Serbs were to enter Srebrenica at the time, that would be a major mistake?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This citation from Mr. Karadzic says that if they - that is the Bosnian Serb forces - had entered Srebrenica, there would have been blood to the knees. And the reason for that was that those entering would be from -- would be those whose families were killed. He foresaw that the entry into Srebrenica could be a bloody and catastrophic event for the Muslims and that the arresting of that process by Morillon probably had more benefits for the Bosnian Serbs because it would have fully discredited them in the eyes of the international community. That's what I see him saying here, and foreseeing that bloodbath which would occur if RS forces entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he says that it would be an error, and the reasons for that is the fact that all Serbs around Srebrenica had been burnt by the forces that were leaving the area, that more than 1.200 Serbs were killed, and that if the people whose families had been killed were to enter, this could have a catastrophic effect. So it is not disputed that the leadership of Republika Srpska is fully conscious that something like that would cause a disaster and that it would be extremely damaging for Republika Srpska as well. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, recognising this is at the time of the 33rd Session in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if someone has an awareness of how disastrous such an act would be for Republika Srpska in 1993, surely they would have the same awareness later on. This awareness could not have changed regarding the significance and disastrous consequences of such an event. If there was awareness of this earlier on, surely that awareness must have continued as to how disastrous and damaging such an act would be. Isn't that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic here is expressing the consequences of this foreseeable slaughter not in terms of the Muslims who might be killed but the fact that it might compromise the security of the Bosnian Serb state by which he, in this context, typically meant its international recognition. This was the case in 1993 when the primary goal of the Bosnian Serb leadership essentially from May 1992 until this time and somewhat further was the international recognition of the Republika Srpska. In 1995, that situation had appreciably changed along with the military situation along the ground, and the threat to Republika Srpska in 1995 came principally from military sources rather than from the lack of diplomatic recognition. So those two contexts, in fact, are quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there's no difference with regard to the fact that there was very clear awareness among the leadership of Republika Srpska that such an event would have a very negative impact on the interests of Republika Srpska, not to go into the interests of those who were the victims, because something like that could only have been done by somebody who was an enemy of both the Muslims and the Serbs, that is, the event of 1995. Someone with a criminal consciousness and someone who is a lunatic. However, here they clearly indicate that they are aware how harmful that would be for Republika Srpska. Isn't that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement here is that it -- we might lose the state for that. And as I've explained, what I think that statement refers to is the dimming of prospects for international recognition. That was the key issue for the Bosnian Serb leadership at this time. By 1995, losing the state meant its being overrun militarily, particularly in Western Bosnia, and therefore, the entire context changed. In this statement, there is no sensitivity, no indication that the consequences of this possible entry would be detrimental to the Muslims. That's not a part of the expression here of concern. The concern is purely one for the existence of the Republika Srpska. But I don't think the interests of the leadership of the Republika Srpska were the same in 1995 as they were in 1993 when the military situation in 1993 was extremely favourable for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting from what you yourself say under the heading "Entering Srebrenica would produce catastrophic results," and I assume you correctly quote from the transcripts. I never saw those transcripts, nor have I read them, nor have I studied them, so the quotation is yours under the sub-heading "Entering Srebrenica would produce catastrophic results," and Karadzic apparently says: "How does that apply to Srebrenica? I think that's a point for us, for if we had entered Srebrenica, the people entering would be those whose families were killed. 1.200 Serbs were killed. There would be blood to the knees and we could lose the state for that. That is why I believe that Morillon saved us, not the Muslims, when he entered Srebrenica." So when he says that there would be a major conflict and that there would be many conflicts proves -- disproves what you said a moment ago. That is, you say that he doesn't mention the victims. On the contrary, he does talk about the victims that in such a terrible situation would necessarily be incurred. Is that in dispute, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these words speak very clearly for themselves. They are not as you suggested, my words. They are Mr. Karadzic's words, and they were taken directly from the statement that he made in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. I've provided a brief summary of the context at the beginning of this, and the rest of the words are Mr. Karadzic's as directly taken from the Assembly minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding between us, Mr. Donia. I didn't say that they were your words but a quotation that you chose, and I even said that I assume that you correctly quoted from the minutes of the speech of Radovan Karadzic, and then you quote him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've exhausted this topic. We've been over it. We can read what the witness has said. It will be for us to determine what effect those words had. We shall move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page ERN 227 is the last number, you quote another speech of Karadzic's under the heading "We must incite incidents to intensify conflict." That is what you put down. And here is what Karadzic says: "It is important that we have pulled out the Serbs from Gorazde. We don't want to open fire on Gorazde. There is no need for us to fire a single bullet at Gorazde. We have won militarily, we must win politically. We must foresee what will happen and preempt the events. The contract signed is disastrous for the Muslims. It is for history. It is recognition of Serb victory, and Morillon signed it." Is that quotation correct, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where did you read that Karadzic said that incidents needed to be incited to intensify the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Centering on the words "inflame these events," which is my English translation as I have it here: "We must foresee what will happen and inflame those events or a day beforehand take measures which will incite senseless measures against us."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't Karadzic speak about political solutions and the absence of the need for waging war? He even says there is no need to fire a single bullet around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is part of his locution here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The 34th Session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, several sessions from the 27th of August to the 1st of October, this is what you say in your report, because I -- I didn't use any other sources except your own report. Is it true that there were three basic topics of this session that took place in seven hearings? Was the peace plan, the plan of union of the three republics, and then analysis of the military rebellion, September 1993, the appeal to Serbian Krajina to send aid because of the attack by Croatian units? Is it true, since you're quoting Karadzic in the first place, that Karadzic had a positive attitude towards the plan of the union of three republics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Karadzic expressed readiness in the interest of a peace agreement for the Serbs to renounce certain parts of the territory that they had under their control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then a chapter headed "Karadzic explains the nature of the relationships with Milosevic." Is it true that in answer to this he says: "I have to tell you that they are cautious with us. They have burnt their fingers. They are very cautious. I can't say that they're not bringing pressure to bear, but not in the form of ultimatums. They talk to us. They are showing a great deal of patience with us." And then he explains that I assisted in particular with respect to the constitutional principles. Anyway, Lord Owen also spoke about my role in connection with those constitutional principles. Are you aware, Mr. Donia, that it was thanks to my own efforts that those constitutional principles were adopted? And once certain principles are adopted by all three parties, isn't that the best proof that the approach taken is an objective one and it is not to the detriment of any one side? So that these were endeavours to find a peaceful solution, in fact. Are you aware of that, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to those generalisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Donia. Tell me, please, on page 03085232, when you're recounting Karadzic's speech, you say that in a rather disconnected sentence he declares that he's expecting a massacre in Sarajevo. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't help me with that. Could you kindly suggest an English language reference? Oh, I see it. I see, it Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is it, please, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the bottom of -- if I look at the ERN number, it's 02989205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 38 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that he expects a massacre in Sarajevo, and you attribute that to Karadzic in interpreting a sentence that was rather disconnected and difficult to understand. Is that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I regret not having cited that sentence even though it was somewhat circumlocuitous. I meant to highlight the fact that in terms of the use of heavy weapons, he was sensitive to constraints of international -- he expressed himself to be sensitive to the constraints of international law and the international media. I could certainly provide or we can identify where that sentence is and get its explicit translation. I don't have that with me, unfortunately, but it can be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a massacre are you talking about in Sarajevo as coming out of that rambling sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to go to the original. I think that he was speaking of a cataclysmic conclusion to Sarajevo events without suggesting that any one side was going to perpetrate that cataclysmic conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had nearly the time which was allotted but we'll give you another five minutes so you can wrap up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I can do in five minutes' time I really don't know, Mr. May. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I'm going to skip over some of the notes I've made here, but on page 003 -- 540 are the last digits. You use the expression "Greater Serbia," and you use it in your chapter heading, and that chapter heading reads as follows: "Greater Serbia Will Integrate Around Belgrade and Regional Centres." Is that right, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in search of an English language citation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is the 35th Assembly session, Mr. Donia, and then there is a sub-heading within the 35th Assembly session. I think that the numbers I have must be different to yours. 240 are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 46, Doctor, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. It is ERN 02989213.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Donia, why did you use the expression "Greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it as a commonly used equivalent of the entire Serbian nation and its integrated form as foreseen by some -- some Serbian intellectuals and policy-makers. I would agree that the term "Velika Srbija" does not appear in the citation, but nevertheless, the sense of that terminology there I think is suitable to use the term "Greater Serbia" there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, are you aware of the fact that not a single representative of the Government of Republika Srpska ever used the term "Greater Serbia" or any plan for a Greater Serbia or anything along those lines nor was our support to peace plans in Bosnia-Herzegovina could be tied with any aspirations to create a Greater Serbia? I hope you know that, Mr. Donia, at least.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would reject that characterisation completely. I think the citations that were cited, or I cited last time in my appearance here, indicated that it was not only an objective but a -- simply assumed objective of the Bosnian Serb leadership to eventually reach integration with other Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, didn't Karadzic say that the overall Serb nation, and he's speaking about the Serb nation, should be integrated around several of its core points, and he speaks about the largest centres in that regard and around Belgrade, to begin with, which is the largest centre, and it's the largest centre in the Balkans, for that matter; a university centre, an administrative centre, an industrial and banking centre, financial centre, scientific centre. In all respects it is a centre. So is it clear to you that Belgrade is the historical, cultural, university, medical, religious, Orthodox centre? It is the starting point, the be-all and end-all of the entire Serb nation for Serbs in America, Australia, Europe, Serbs throughout the world in fact. I assume you know that as an historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're taking up a lot of time on a very simple point. Yes. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Karadzic doesn't say that here, but I would concur of the -- on the importance of Belgrade as a centre in the Balkans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, is it true and correct that Karadzic said, and I think that that is at the 42nd Assembly session, in your analysis of that, he says: "We know for sure that we have to give up something --" so they have to give something. That is without any doubt. "-- if we wish to realise the first strategic goal, and that is to get rid of the enemy in our own home." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have one minute left, Mr. Milosevic. This is in the report, 42nd Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he makes that statement, and I think it is indeed almost a summary of the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership from April 1992 until late 1994, that some territory will probably have to be given up in order to secure the first goal, and that first strategic goal, of course, was the creation of a separate Serbian polity that achieved international recognition. And many people in the Bosnian Serb Assembly were not prepared, were not eager to give up such territory, but that was what the leadership, specifically Messrs. Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic felt was required in order to achieve that first strategic goal, which was a separate community divided completely from Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where does Karadzic mention driving out the Croats and Muslims from their homes at all? Where does he say that at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I believe this was a -- the subject of an errata which I submitted with a translation that is provided in the supplement to the report, and it is a faulty translation for which I take responsibility. I'll find the page in the supplementary report in a minute. Let me see. I think it's the last page. On page 9. On page 9 of the supplement to the report -- and I do not have, Mr. President, the ERN number on the copy I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's ERN ending 5362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I highlighted page 64, note number 133, and offered this correct -- more correct translation: "That is beyond doubt insofar as we want to achieve the first strategic goal, which is to rid our house of the enemy, that is the Croats and Muslims, so that we will no longer be together in a state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now the amicus. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, since my time as an amicus is very limited, I should like to ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber certain aspects having to do with four paragraphs of your report, and I should like to start with the 39th Assembly session, the English version is on page 56, and it is the 39th Assembly session of Republika Srpska, in actual fact, held on the 24th of March -- 24th to the 25th of March, 1994, and would you focus your attention on the following paragraph: The title is "Karadzic: I am responsible for all army decisions." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is ERN 02989233. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9223, yes. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll focus your attention on the English version. So in this case, it is page 56 of your English text. This is what you say. We have the heading, the title, and further down in the text, as you quote Karadzic, it says the following in inverted commas: "I am responsible to you and the people and the commanders are responsible to me," et cetera, et cetera. And then it says: "I sign. I decide -- that I sign, decide and am responsible for every decision." Is that right? Further down in the text. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So is that a little different from what it says that he is responsible for every decision of the army? He says that he is responsible for each of the decisions he signs and where his signature exists, the decisions signed by him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the essence of his statement is that he accepts responsibility for all army decisions and explains that on the basis of his having -- he assumes responsibility for having formed the high command and agrees in not hiding behind it that he is indeed accepting responsibility for its decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But only the decisions he himself signs, puts his signature to. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in saying that "not that I hide behind high command" goes beyond saying that only those things that he signs and decides are his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at your report on page 75, the English. It is the 52nd Assembly session, and it says: "Karadzic issued a written and oral order to take control of Srebrenica." Now, I can't quote everything, but he stands behind directive 7 and he expressly states that, and we've already dealt with that directive, it was brought up by the OTP, but somewhere in the middle of that paragraph he mentions Tolimir and then says that: "Tolimir is encouraging the army to persevere. While people didn't say to me, Hey, man, he wants to intervene in this order in order to say that you weren't for it." Now, did you find that in the documents and is that -- was it how it is stated here in your report? Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have the Serbian original, I believe, in the footnote, so that would be the way it was stated by him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to page 83 of the English version. It is the 54th Assembly session, and the paragraph is entitled: "Karadzic Signed Seven Directives which were put before him -- Submitted to him." And in that paragraph, you state under quotation marks that he said the following: "I looked over, approved and signed seven directives. The eighth and ninth were not submitted to me by anyone, nor did I read them let alone sign them. That is because General Gvero wrote and those others who should listen to this. I will not tolerate this." Is that something that you came across in the documents as being ascribed to Karadzic, Karadzic having said that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we have here, and it's already been put forward before this Trial Chamber in tab 2, in actual fact, 553, Rupert Smith, that is directive number 7. It was introduced into court through Rupert Smith. And I'd like to draw your attention to what the directive says. The Prosecutor has already shown us this in a single sentence with respect to the Drina Corps, and it is to be found on page 10 of the directive. It is the last paragraph. I have the directive here, directive 7. Would you please take a look at page 10 and the last paragraph on that English version page. And it refers to the Drina Corps. And the Prosecutor quoted a sentence from that. I'm not going to go back to that sentence. It is also to be found in that portion. But what is referred to here is the fact that the -- that with an active and persistent defence, breakthroughs should be prevented of the enemy. And then at the end it says that the opposite side should be thwarted and war plans are what is referred to, that the enemy should be routed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what is your question? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph of that directive, is mention made of the fact that certain territories should be defended mostly, and does it refer to military operations by and large?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Military operations with stark consequences for civilian inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I won't interpret it myself. Every -- we can read what it says, and the Judges can too. There was another piece of evidence produced here in Rupert Smith's testimony, and it is 553 in tab 3, which refers to the operational elaboration of that particular directive. I have the document of that as well, and I'm sure you've had occasion to see it, but you can take a look at it here and now. It is the directive for further operations and the elaboration of the previous directive given by Karadzic, and this one is signed by Ratko Mladic. Now, take a look at point 1. The basic characteristics of the military and political situation. That is the heading. And then it says: "From the beginning of the year, and especially in the second half of the month of March, the Muslim forces have synchronised their approach to a flagrant violation of the four-month truce agreement." Have you had a chance of seeing that and did you link it up to the operative that -- and operation that the Prosecutor asked you about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is two questions there. Have I seen it? No, I have not seen this document before you gave it to me. And second, did I link it up with this statement of Karadzic or with the operation? No, that's not been my -- my intent has not been to do that but to sort of let the leaders of the Bosnian Serb Assembly speak for themselves in regard to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a lot of material there, and Their Honours can take a look at what it says about the various groupings at the front. Their Honours can read that for themselves. But what I am going to read out is point 2 of that same document. It is on the next page. "The tasks of the army of Republika Srpska on the basis of directive number 7, the army of Republika Srpska has as its task to be persistent in its defence on all areas of the battlefield and to defend the territory of Republika Srpska." Were you able to place that in the context of everything else that you were able to read in the minutes from the Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've indicated, that has not been my intent in this piece. I deliberately did not include any references to other documents, either press reports or various chronologies or things. That would have been an absolutely enormous task. So no, I have not sought to link this particular document to the Bosnian Serb Assembly deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, I just have two more matters to address. I think I will get through them in several minutes. I am convinced and you know we amicus did not conduct any investigations of our own, nor is that our job nor could we have done so. However, I am quite convinced that the OTP must have this book here which was published several months ago, and I would like to see if in actual fact Mr. Donia has had a chance of coming across this book and reading it, because they are orders, all the orders issued by Mr. Karadzic himself. I should like to focus on two orders which have been translated into English, and this book does exist both in Serbian and in English. It is all -- contains all Karadzic's orders. I would like to refer to the one of the 11th of July, 1995, those orders of that particular day. The date is the 11th of July, 1995, which is when the attack on Srebrenica started. Just two, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see if the witness can help at all. It may be that he doesn't know anything about this. Dr. Donia, you have heard of what Tapuskovic has said. Do you know anything about what he is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I'm not familiar with the work that he's citing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that you can find a witness who could deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if all the decisions and documents exist, the ones that Mr. Donia looked at -- because you dealt with written documents, as far as I understand it. Here we have two decisions passed on the 11th of July signed by Radovan Karadzic which have to do with the order to the appointment of the commissars, Miroslav Deronjic, in actual fact, who was to have seen to respect of the humanitarian orders. And both are dated the 11th of July. So it would be a good idea to have a look at them, to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you have not, Mr. Donia, then we can perhaps wait for another witness to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the very point. Let's wait for another witness and we can deal with it with him or her. Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had another question, Your Honours. One more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it is to do with page 72 of the English version. It is the 52nd Assembly session, and it discusses the problems of Srebrenica and Zepa and an order by General Gvero in that respect, and he says: "At the time when the Drina Corps at the Sarajevo battlefront and when we did not bring in the unit -- this was a time when the same Drina Corps gave up a brigade to the Sarajevo front and when we couldn't spare either a MUP unit or a unit from other zones of responsibility except from the Drina Corps." Did you find a single piece of evidence or fact to show that any commander called a unit of the army of Yugoslavia to take part in any operation whatsoever linked to these areas and regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's my first question. My second question is: Now, was the case quite different when it came to Croatia? Could you answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your second question, I'm not too sure what that refers to, different in Croatia. I'm unable to understand what you're asking me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information to the effect that on the side of the Bosnian Croats, on the Bosnian Muslims, when there was moving across the territory to Serbian Krajina, whether there were Croatian military units involved. And the orders which have to do with the work of the Drina Corps, we see that no unit of the army of Yugoslavia ever took part, nor was it called upon to do so.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was your first question. The second question as to Croatia, I haven't addressed here nor am I in a position, not being a military expert, to address what units were or were not in Bosnia in July of 1995. As to -- your first question really is about the documents about the army of Yugoslavia. I have not sought nor am aware of such documents. I'm sure that they exist in the archives of -- those roles are probably explained in the archives of Serbia which, unfortunately, are not open to investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. In the quotation that you yourself quote, it is General Gvero who says that he did not call upon any other unit, not only of the army of Yugoslavia but no other MUP unit or unit from other zones of responsibility except for the Serb army in Bosnia. So the army of Yugoslavia is not mentioned here at all and that is not what I asked you. The Drina Corps only deployed units of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I am saying, according to this quote, of the Serb army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can read what it says. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I would like to return to the 30 the Assembly session and in particular to the words of Mr. Milosevic, and that is Exhibit 538, tab 9. The text will be displayed on the screen in front of you. If I could ask the usher to adjust it for the Sanction system. I want to direct your attention to five different sentences in Mr. Milosevic's second address to that Assembly session and I want to ask you to put them into context for us. The first passage you've already testified about previously. I want to draw your attention to a particular part of it. It begins with: "The question was asked, which I really find unacceptable: Whether we give up on our goal? I shall tell you no, we do not give up on our goal." Then just reading the last line of that paragraph: "The goal was completed in many aspects but not in all of them but it represents a way towards the ultimate goal, of course it does." Now, when Mr. Milosevic said, "The goal was completed in many aspects but not in all of them," you testified previously about how the word "goal" would have been interpreted. Can I ask you to place in context or what can be reasonably concluded from Mr. Milosevic saying, "but not all of them." What aspects of that goal at the time that he was making this address in May of 1993, what aspects of the goal were still yet to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in the context in which he was speaking, the only thing that can be concluded about "the goal" is that it referred to the unity of Serbs in some polity. What was at that time not yet completed was the integration of Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina in a single territorial unit nor the integration of Serbs on a broader basis, that is to include the Republika Srpska Krajina, those Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A few sentences below that passage I want to direct your attention to another line, and again it will be displayed before you. Mr. Milosevic says: "The question arises, who has the right to choose the unreasonable losses, the huge losses in the name of the people?" Can it be reasonably concluded from this passage that in Mr. Milosevic's view, a rejection of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan would have resulted in unreasonable losses, in huge losses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next line I would like to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Groome. Could you give the tab number of the document. Is it tab 9 of 538?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it is page 96 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document we are given consists of 116 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, this is on page 96 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next line I would like to draw your attention to, and again it's a few sentences below that last passage, is Mr. Milosevic says: "If we preserve our people and territories, we shall win these factories easily." What can be reasonably concluded from Mr. Milosevic's reference to "our people"? Who would he be referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few paragraphs before this, or a few sentences before this, Mr. Milosevic began -- begins to use the plural first person "we" or its grammatical equivalent in Serbian. And for essentially the rest of this address, he continues to use the term "we." And that "we" is first used or used early on in regard to the Bosnian Serbs. He speaks collectively of himself and the Bosnian Serbs and speaks of himself in the role of the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. And this is one sentence in a series -- or several sentences in which he actually speaks in that first person plural of going beyond the specific provisions of the Vance-Owen Plan to further steps to consolidate Serbian authority and establish Serbian gains in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next line I'd like to draw your attention to is again just a few lines below that, where Mr. Milosevic says -- and I'm now referring to page 97 of Exhibit 538, tab 9: "The question is especially asked now how are we going to amalgamate the economy of the Serb provinces?" What can be reasonably concluded from his use of the word "Serb provinces"? What territories would he have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's reasonable to conclude in this context that he is speaking of the various polities in which Serbs reside, to include the Republika Srpska Krajina, Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, Republic of Montenegro, and the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And a few lines below that, Mr. Milosevic says: "Serb lands shall belong economically, culturally, educationally and in every other respect. Karadzic spoke about the same primer, et cetera. Accordingly, I suppose it doesn't take too much imagination to realise to where this process is heading." What can be reasonably concluded from Mr. Milosevic's statement that it doesn't take too much imagination to realise where this process is heading? Where is the process heading?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, the process is heading toward the unification, unity of the Serb people in a single polity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last sentence I would ask or seek your comment on is further down on that page - and again it will be displayed before you -

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC SAYS
utterances.text: "And not to realise the tragic mistake that would brutally cut off our way to success, is the Assembly going to decide on the reasonable way or the unreasonable way to the goal?" What can be -- what can we conclude from his interpretation of what is the reasonable way towards the goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasonable way to the goal in this context is the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and the acceptance of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and subsequent steps to consolidate Serbian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the unreasonable way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the unreasonable way is in this context to reject the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Considering these words in the historical context of the time and in the context of the debate that preceded his words, do his words reflect a person who has fundamental disagreement with the goals of those members of the RS Assembly who oppose the Vance-Owen Peace Plan or do they reflect someone who shares the fundamental goals of those opposing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and has strong disagreement with them regarding the best strategy or means of achieving those goals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These goals are shared by the Bosnian Serb leadership and Mr. Milosevic. This is a person who expresses the sense of a common goal with the Bosnian Serbs, and the course of action to reach that goal is what is in fact in question in these locutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- just a moment. Dr. Donia, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This 30th Session proceeded under I think very intense international media scrutiny, and in the course of this 17-hour debate underwent a very significant change in context. We have last time noted -- I believe Mr. Milosevic read in full his opening comments which cited the importance of or the notion that the goals of freedom and equality of the Serbian people had been reached in the Vance-Owen Plan. Thereafter, the very lively discussion which was somewhat typical in the Bosnian Serb Assembly took place, and the -- a number of things were said directly to Mr. Milosevic. Among others, that two delegates mentioned the idea that they had been deserted or betrayed by the leaders of Serbia and Montenegro, and two different persons in the Assembly directly addressing Mr. Milosevic spoke of soldiers dying with pictures of him on their breasts. Mr. Branko Simic said, "Mr. Milosevic you have the love of the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Every soldier that we buried in the valley of the Neretva as a rule had a photo of you on his chest." That is on page 34 of this English translation of the session. The B/C/S ERN is 02150137. And then General Bogdan Subotic said, "Soldiers are dying with your portraits on their T-shirts." This was followed by another, a second speech by Yugoslav president Dobrica Cosic in which he reiterated his earlier formulation of the shared goals of Serbian people everywhere, namely, that the ultimate liberation and unification of the Serbs which he had earlier ascribed to something formulated over two centuries and which had been -- in which -- to achieve those objectives, this was the seventh war that had been fought to fight them. And he said: "There is nothing more urgent and sacred today than fighting for unity and creating conditions to preserve that unity." Then there was a lengthy speech by General Mladic in which he emphasised the thought that the enemies of the Bosnian Serbs had the most up-to-date weapons devised by the mind of man and that the Serbs had nothing. It was then in this context, after these comments, that Mr. Milosevic spoke a second time, and the entire tenor of this was vastly different from his opening remarks. In this second speech, he goes from assuming that the mission has been accomplished to stating that it is partly done and many other things remain to be done. He also changes into this first person plural and speaks somewhat alternately as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs and indeed at one point says that "We should have local authority, our own police, et cetera." Speaking of the areas in Bosnia. That's on page 95 of the document, B/C/S ERN 02150190. There is then one sentence that has not been translated into English in his speech, and if I could read the Serbian, I believe that should be inserted immediately after this statement about "We should have local authority, our own police, et cetera," and that is: [Interpretation] "Those are reserved areas which through the process are gaining in size, are being stabilised, and placed in such a function." [In English] So another feature of this speech is that he is thinking beyond the Vance-Owen Plan and presenting to the audience various steps that can be taken which will effectively supersede and perhaps even undermine the Vance-Owen Plan through these additional steps. And of course there is no further mention in this speech of freedom and equality as the goals of the Serbian people but, rather, this implicit use of the term "goal" as unification of all Serbs. This, to me, is a very significant change in tenor and one which spoke both to the environment in Pale at that time and the objective that the Bosnian Serbs and Mr. Milosevic shared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Very briefly now because we are beyond our time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. Donia has just now presented a whole series of entirely distorted interpretations of my speeches. As I spoke at that session twice, I am not going to repeat what I said. He speaks about goals, and I have here a newspaper issued on that same date which I wish to tender into evidence and from which it can be seen that I say quite clearly: "What is the goal of the Serbian people in the Balkans? I would say very briefly: The goal of the Serbian people in the Balkans has been and remains to be free and equal." And then I explain other reasons why the Vance-Owen Plan should be adopted and why it would be unreasonable and so on not to adopt it. Please can I have this admitted into evidence? These are newspapers from that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's an absolutely clear interpretation rather than these nebulous sentences taken out of context. Secondly, in my second speech, which came, as Mr. Donia said, after a very lively and emotional discussion indeed and which was quite brief, I say that I will tell them what I think with the greatest responsibility but also my impressions. I say to them: "You have spoken openly and from the heart." And this was quite clear, because that session was highly emotional and heated. "Most of what you said refers to the cruelty and injustices of war," because people spoke of the terrible crimes against the Serb people. And I say: "Throughout the history of the Serbian people there are too many truthful testimonies of the horrors of war, but all that we have heard today regarding testimony," and I speak in the first person plural, yes, that those of us here have heard, we, we sitting at that Assembly session. "All that we have heard about the horrors of war can all be united to form one single argument and one single statement and message, and that is that the war must stop as soon as possible. The war must stop immediately." So after all these emotional statements, I interpret everything that has been said, that it should form a single statement, a single message, and that is that the war must cease immediately. And then I go on to say what and how things should be done, and I say: "The Assembly must have the courage and the self-confidence under these circumstances on whatever basis we have, but a sufficient basis provided by the Vance-Owen Plan to achieve our goal rather than making the tragic mistake which will truly obstruct the path to success. Whether the Assembly will choose the reasonable or unreasonable path to the goal, surely no one needs to persuade the Assembly, because for me, peace is the reasonable path. Otherwise, under the slogan that only the Serbs don't want peace, crimes can be committed against the Serbs under that slogan. You cannot, now that the path is being opened to peace, explain to the people why it should go on losing its lives -- their lives more cruelly than throughout the war. You cannot explain that to the people of Republika Srpska or the people of Serbia." That is my second speech. And the first one I wish -- I have tendered as an exhibit, and I have tendered already this second one, and I think that after Lord Owen's testimony, there is no point. It is senseless to try and interpret the Assembly meetings in Pale. So please can I tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can tender it into evidence. It will get the next D number. It will be for us to interpret what those various statements mean. I have allowed you to respond because allegations were made against you, but it will be for the Court to determine. Yes. We will have the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit number is 213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Donia, thank you for coming back. Your evidence is concluded. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D number should be corrected as 214. Please check it out during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take a seat. Witness B-1097, you are, of course, still under the declaration which you took on the last occasion. I remind the Court and for the record note that this witness has given evidence in July. He was examined-in-chief, cross-examined for some time. Nonetheless, there was half an hour's cross-examination still outstanding when the witness fell -- the accused, rather, fell ill, and it is, therefore, for the accused to continue his cross-examination for that amount of time, and I thank the witness for returning. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1097, did the first incident occur on the 31st of May when Omer Selimovic, who was one of the soldiers in the Muslim army, clashed with other Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no incident on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the separation line there was very fierce shooting?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 14, you say: "Omer Selimovic, one of the soldiers of the Muslim army, came to Klisa where we were staying for the night with some relatives. He came with other Muslim soldiers and told the men to go with them to the free territory. We set off with them, about 100 of us. At the confrontation line, there were several machine-gun nests, and the shooting was fierce," et cetera. So then how can you say that there was no shooting along the confrontation line when you said quite the opposite in your statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Omer Selimovic had come to pull out the people, to save the people. As we didn't manage to leave, he stayed and he pulled out together with the army later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was there heavy shooting or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Serbian side, yes, whereas our Territorial Defence did not shoot at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there was heavy shooting along the separation line.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're now explaining that it was from the Serbian side, which means only the Serbs were shooting and you were not.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were civilians. We didn't have any weapons. The few soldiers there were didn't open fire. There was no shooting from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1097, you explain -- you describe the people to whom you surrendered. You say that they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they had no insignia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you personally recognised some people who were present when they took you into custody. You mention quite a large number of people. Were they all people from your area whom you knew and you knew their names?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I knew these people from the neighbouring village, but there were quite a number that I didn't know who were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know they were from Serbia? Just because you didn't know them? You listed many of those you knew.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was -- these were active soldiers who were dressed properly, whereas our local ones didn't have complete uniforms. They were unshaven and disorderly, as opposed to those active soldiers who were very orderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clear up something. You say that the soldiers on the bridge wore camouflage caps which you had never seen before, that they took away Dzemail Djulic, and that the Serbs beat those people with baseball bats and other objects. First let me ask you, where did those baseball bats come from in Bosnia where no one over there has such an implement as a baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen them before. There were baseball bats, batons, iron poles and other instruments they used to beat the men with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You insist that they used baseball bats to beat the people with.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; baseball bats, iron poles and truncheons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that those who were beating could not have been regular army members?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that among them there were active-duty soldiers, and there were locals as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could active-soldiers get mixed up with these others in such a disorganised manner?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was disorganised or not, but there were active-duty officers and soldiers mixed together with these others. I don't know how to describe them. That's not a question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you describe the people who took you to Karakaj, is it true that the local Serbs had olive-green uniforms and camouflage caps and wore various insignia?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some in olive-green winter uniforms though it was summer. They were not all uniformly dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't that tell you at least that they couldn't have been JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, Mr. Milosevic, that with them there were some active-duty troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But people wearing winter uniforms in July with no patches and dressed in different ways certainly could not have been JNA members.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there were JNA officers and soldiers there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
