utterances.text: Is it true that you recognised the persons who were there? You mentioned Vidovic and his father's name and a certain Arapovic and Pejic and a number of others that you mention. Someone who had a house next to the technical school in Karakaj and worked in Sperploca company, a machine technician who had a house across the street. You mention his brother, his mother. All these things that you mention seems to indicate that these were local people. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about those that I don't know. I just know that they were active duty officers. As for the others, they were my colleagues from work and that's why I know them by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that they released you, let you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them needed to release you, but anyway, you were let free?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man, a man I used to work with, released me, let me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw one soldier who was the only one who was wearing a JNA uniform with a five-cornered star on his cap. So he wasn't with any JNA unit. But regardless of the uniform he was wearing, he was a local from Karakaj, and his name was Stevanovic. Is that right or not? You say he had a house close to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "He was the only one I saw with a Red Star."

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it clear, then, regardless of the uniform he was wearing, you say he was the only one with such a uniform. So surely he couldn't have been in any JNA unit but just a local who happened to be there and was -- put on a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, Mr. Milosevic, but one of the active-duty soldiers travelled with me to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who saved you?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what then?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the officers or soldiers. I don't know exactly what rank he had. He happened to travel with me from Sabac to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Sabac is in Serbia as is Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I took a regular bus from Loznica to Sabac, and that same bus was going from Zvornik to Novi Sad. He got in Zvornik, so we travelled together in the same bus. He was sitting on the back seat of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you concluded from that, from the fact that you were travelling on the same bus, a regular public transport bus, what -- so you got on the same bus and travelled together. What did you conclude from that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was a soldier, that he was travelling to Novi Sad. He spoke the Ekavian dialect, and I know that he was an officer. He was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was in uniform. He was travelling through Serbia. What connection does he have with the events over there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he has when he was one of the security officers in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say he was the only one in a JNA uniform, but he was also a local.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that he was wearing an old SMB uniform, whereas the others, this gentleman, had a regular camouflage uniform of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now, give me a direct answer. You didn't witness any executions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any executions.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No mass, large-scale executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any individual executions?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. They didn't kill people in our presence except for two killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any executions?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, Mr. Milosevic. I didn't see any group executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But not a single one either?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They killed one man with an automatic rifle, who had taken an electric cable to kill himself, they killed the man and took him out of the room. That's the only thing I saw. And I saw a man without his head. His brothers claimed that he had been killed. His name was Emir Selimovic. I couldn't recognise him, but his brothers recognised him by the clothing he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that one day a Chetnik duke called Rakic from the village of Cer arrived who used to work in the engineering company in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was known because he was making bricks at home, and they called him Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he said that he would kill the balijas. That is the expression he used; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He made you sing songs.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Alija, if there's war, we will slaughter you like Milos slaughtered Murat." Those were the words of that one song that we sang.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues...] didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this man, the way you describe him, what he did, where he was, where he came from, wasn't from Serbia nor did he belong to any of the Yugoslav armed forces. Is that quite clear or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from that hell hole, you escaped to a safe place and that was Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no choice, because they didn't let me go to Tuzla or where my family lived. All they said -- he said was that I could go the other way and asked me whether I had anybody in Serbia. And I said yes, I did, my sister-in-law, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you went to a safe place, and that safe place was Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was safe. I had no choice, because I don't -- Serbia wasn't too safe for me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't anybody mistreat you in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody know who I was or where I was from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked you at all, did they. Nobody stopped you or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no problems. Nobody knew who I was, I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you crossed into Serbia to Mali Zvornik, Loznica, Sabac, and went on to Novi Sad where you put up finally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then without any problems at all you asked for a passport there, to be issued a passport. You received a passport and could go wherever you wanted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is that then something that clearly indicates that not only did you have no problems when you were in Serbia but somebody had to ask you where you were from and who you were if you were issued a passport. And once they had learnt that, nobody made any problems either?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for me personally but other people did have problems at this private camp in Subotica, and I heard that people had problems over there, but I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard people had problems?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at the technical school in Karakaj, your relations were being held captive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My entire family, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to them then?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's a question for me to answer. It's a question that you can ask the people, and I'm sure you know that a grave has been discovered with 600 bodies at Crni Vrh and some of the bodies have been exhumed, and they acknowledged that they killed some of them, my father and cousins and so on, but their bodies were not all found, and the DNA analysis is being conducted. Certain bodies were found but my father's body was not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't know whether they're alive or not because they're listed as missing persons?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The authorities confirmed, of Republika Srpska, that they are not among the living, and if he had just been on the missing persons' list he wouldn't have been able to receive a pension and they recognised that these people had been killed and a mass grave discovered and some 100 corpses have been identified to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1097, where was this mass grave uncovered, near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Crni Vrh, at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters have asked me to slow down. I'll do so. Now, you've just said that they owned up to killing them. Who owned up to the fact that these were killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities of Republika Srpska, and on television, the president of the municipality personally attended the exhumation proceedings, and it was acknowledged that they had been killed and that 600 corpses had been uncovered, and of those 600, 100 or so were from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as I don't have any information as to what was going on there, could you tell me now, since you're speaking about this matter and say that the president of the municipality appeared on television and said that these people had been killed and so on and so forth, whether anything is known about who the perpetrators were? Who committed the crimes? Who killed these people? Was that part of the information you were given too? Did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you not understanding me or don't you want to understand me? The president of the municipality attended the exhumation, and one or two years prior to that it had already been recognised on the part of the authorities that these people had been killed, whereas the mayor, as a mark of respect to the casualties, attended the exhumation procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, I'm sure that when a mayor does attend an exhumation ceremony it is out of respect for the casualties, but you said that these people had been killed and that the authorities recognised that they had been killed. Now, can you tell us who killed those people?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. The Serbs killed them. Now, whether it was done by the active army or by the paramilitary formations or whoever else, I don't know. I didn't see it happen, so I can't say, and I'm not going to say something I didn't see happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So are the perpetrators known or are you just saying that you don't know who the killers are?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Probably those people do know, but I don't know who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1097. Now, answer this, please. I have a few more questions for you relating to the events that took place in your region. Already at the beginning of the conflict in your area, was the Patriotic League active?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me this, please: Who was at the head of this Patriotic League? Who led it? And what -- how many men did that formation number?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of men, but I -- and I don't know the man personally. I've just heard his name and that his name was Hajrudin Mesic and that this was his unit. I can't tell you any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was the League's headquarters at Kula Grad near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you happen to know whether it is true and correct that as of January 1992, along the streets of Zvornik, many criminals could be seen walking around wearing police uniforms on the streets of Zvornik and that the fighters for the faith, led by the well-known Zvornik criminal Midhat Grakic, began to appear around that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know anything about the Mosque Doves, the Dzamijski Golubovi unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't heard about the Mosque Doves?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just heard it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the Zvornik area, in addition to this Patriotic League, was there another Muslim paramilitary group called the Kobra commanded by a man named Suljo who used to be a teacher before the war in Sapra [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about that group called the Kobras at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how about the Zvornik Brigade of the army of Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 28764 to 28777. Bosnia-Herzegovina? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the immediate cause for the conflict in Zvornik, was it the mobilisation of the Muslim militia, police, which was ordered by the president of the municipality and Abdulah Pasic, a former dentist, and Nedzad Sabic, the commander of the TO headquarters and staff?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: Was the immediate cause of the conflict in Zvornik the mobilisation of the Muslim police which was ordered by the president of the municipality and a deputy of the Party of Democratic Action, a former dentist by the name of Abdulah Pasic and Nedzad Sabic, commander of the TO headquarters, the Territorial Defence, who was later on the commander of the 1st Podrinje Brigade of the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the cause. At least I don't believe it was, but I don't really know about things like that. And I haven't heard of those names ever before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question as to the immediate cause and whether it was caused by the mobilisation of the Muslim police, was it that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean there wasn't any Muslim mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, do you know this, that the Serbian village of Boskovic in Zvornik, the Muslims on the 5th of May 1992 launched an attack on which occasion they killed the majority of the Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was killed, Mr. Milosevic, on that occasion nor was there an attack. I've never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you happen to recall that the paramilitary formations of the Muslims would attack the suburbs of Zvornik at night and loot and attack Serb houses and ransack Serb flats? For example, of the 17th of April, 1992, there was an attack on the Serbian village of Rastosnica, in the Zvornik municipality. And I have here a piece of information telling me that Bogdanovic Zoran was killed, and his father's name was Petar. He was born in 1971. Then another village that was looted and burned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know about that, Mr. Milosevic, I never heard that having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the 5th of May, Boskovic, where nine Serbs were killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm hearing that for the first time. They killed hundreds of people there in the Muslim village of Vitinci and they kept shelling the village. That I do know. But that there were any attacks on the villages you mention, I don't know about that. I'm hearing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what about the 9th of May, Gornja Baljkovica was attacked and 16 Serbs were killed and then the Serb village was looted and burnt. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know it's not true?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have heard about it from someone and I've never heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't heard about it? All right. Fine. Now, do you happen to remember a May 1992 attack against the village of Rozanj, right up until September when the locals were finally forced to leave the village, and tens of people were killed during that attack, and the Serbian village of Rozanj was completed looted and burnt?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. Milosevic. It's 40 kilometres away from me, and I had no freedom of movement so how could I know what was going on in that part? It had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you don't know about it and then you said it wasn't correct. What about the 1st of August in the Boskovici region when 26 Serbs were killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm hearing about that for the first time. All I do know is that all the coordination kept from -- came from this village of Boskovici. The attacks on the village of Bistrinici, that's where it was coordinated. That's what I heard about, but I didn't hear about the massacre there or anything else that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, as time is running out: I don't want to remind you of all the events that took place, but do you know about this one at Snagovo, Kamenica, Crni Vrh, Novo Selo, Setici, Jusici, and so on and so forth when major crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about the crime in Jusici where about 40 Muslims were killed when the Serb army entered the village and killed about 40 civilians. That is what I did hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, all the villages that I mentioned, I gave you their names because my information tells me that the crimes were committed against the Serbs in all these villages. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's incorrect information, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that it wasn't Serbs who were killed in those villages and that those villages weren't burnt or looted and that none of that is correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that. I'm saying I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that the forces of the Territorial Defence, as they were called then, the Muslim forces under the command of Hajrudin Mesic, in actual fact, arrived in your village in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were there yourself, were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, through their conduct, did this lead to inter-ethnic tension?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the tension didn't arise because they came. They wanted to protect us, to pull the people out, and people withdrew without incident. But that wasn't the reason. So I think that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that Alija Djulic and Ibrahim Majlovic told you to hand over two official pistols to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that Captain Dzemal Spahic, the commander of the TO from Handelici in Vitnica, brought in about 100 men to your village? Dzemal Spahic, was he a former JNA captain? You've received information to that effect? Well, is it true?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1097, I apologise if I repeat my questions again to you once I've already asked you, but you testified rather a long time ago, so I might have got this mixed up.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm fully aware of what I talked about and the questions you asked me, and I think that I've answered most of those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a JNA captain, was he, this man who came in with 100 men?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it -- he sent by the JNA to go there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you think that this other man you saw who was a Serb was sent by the JNA, then, if this man of yours -- if for him you claim that the JNA did not send him, why do you claim that the JNA sent the Serbian who was outside this military formation?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he -- the man came to protect the people, to save them and pull the people out of the area. Now, the other men who came to escort us killed all the people in the camps. Nobody left the camps alive. So if you claim something to the contrary, you have a list of 700 men. There were even more men. There were about a thousand people, and none of them except for four men left the camp alive. Even ten years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything about the events that went on there, because quite simply I don't know anything about those events, and they have nothing to do with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you do, sir. You watched it all on television. You saw the incidents take place. It was televised by Serb television and Serb television studio Sabac in fact filmed the camps and the whole of Serbia was able to watch it on television. It seems that just you, Mr. Milosevic, weren't able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now the fact that what you're claiming, that the whole of Serbia saw it on television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that formation later attacked Cilovo Brdo, which is close by your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you got that piece of information, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it is true or not.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the attack was launched at 9.00 in the morning and you and half the other men from the village took part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times you want me to repeat what I've already said. You're asking me about something that happened a long time ago. You got an answer from me three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. The witness has dealt with this particular attack once already. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just dealing with some questions, Witness, that Mr. Milosevic has been asking you about Hajrudin Mesic, who was the Muslim TO commander. I'm looking at paragraph 4 of your Rule 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible that the witness may be provided with a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, the time that Hajrudin Mesic came to your area was in May of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before then, there had been no fighting in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hajrudin Mesic came with a group of armed people from the Muslim TO. What was the exact status and position of Hajrudin Mesic? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Crveni Mulj dam and the Glinica factory refuse was collected at the dam, there was speculations that it would be blown up, so they took positions for this not to happen and provided security for the Glinica factory. The Territorial Defence took up pistols and protected the dam to prevent it from being blown up and to protect the civilian population, because they weren't able to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I asked you was: Who was Hajrudin Mesic? Was he a commander of the Muslim TO before the conflict? Was he from that local area?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't from the local area. I think he was from Teocak or, rather, that's where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before he arrived in your area with the Muslim TO, do you know what he was doing earlier?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? I didn't hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hajrudin Mesic arrives in your area with a group of armed people from the Muslim TO, and there had been no conflict in your area before he came. What I want to find out from you was how it was that he came to that area, what his authority was. And as part of that background, can you tell us, if you know, what he did before. Was he in the JNA? Did he have any specific functional role in the military?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what functional role he had and what he did before that, and I don't want to guess. As to what people said, well, I really don't know what role he had in the army or the police or wherever. All I know is that he came with the purpose of protecting the people and to protect the Crveni Mulj dam, to prevent an ecological catastrophe from the industrial waste that was collecting there. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As it was, then, some members of his armed group asked you to surrender your pistols to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why didn't you resist giving up your pistols to this group of armed people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We appear to be having some technical problems. Just a moment. Yes. If you would repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why didn't you resist giving up your weapons to this group?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the regular Territorial Defence, and it never entered my head to refuse doing what they had asked us, because the entire village handed over the weapons to the Serbs, and they said that we should hand over these official pistols. And they were returned once they had withdrawn from the area. The pistols were returned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As far as the dam is concerned, was it the Muslim TO who made the threat to blow up the dam and said that they had mined it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dam was not mined. The pipes bringing in the silt below the dam was what was mined. The dam was not mined. But later on over television, the Republic of Serbia showed that the dam had been mined, and that was not correct. It was just the pipes to the -- at the entrance to the dam that were blown up -- that were mined. I don't know what actually happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you answer the first part --

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as a preventative measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you answer the first part of the question: Was it the Muslim TO who made that threat to mine the dam?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present. I didn't hear about that. But I did hear from others that threats were made to the effect that they would blow up the dam. And the information media had already broadcast that, but it wasn't true. What could we mine it with when we handed over the weapons and there wasn't any explosive? Possibly some threats were made but it never came to anything. And I know that to be true 100 per cent. The dam was not mined. It was just these entrance pipes that were mined, entrance to the dam. For you to blow up the whole dam you would need a whole lot of explosives and that would be all nigh impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 7 of your statement and I'll ask the question just one more time. If you could answer it, please. Was it the Muslim TO who made the threat to blow up the dam? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it the Muslim TO who made the threat to blow up the dam?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that. I don't know. All I heard is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at your statement, it says in paragraph 7: "One day, the TO telephoned one of the officers, I cannot tell who he was, in the Glinica factory and threatened that the TO would blow up the dam which had previously been mined." The question was: Was that a threat from the Muslim TO?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the people threatening, the people from the village, from that village. And we didn't hand over Hajrudin Mesic to his people but to the locals of the village, and those official pistols Ibrahim Majlovic and Djulic. That's who we surrendered our pistols to. Now, which of those people spoke over the phone, I really can't say, I don't know, to the effect that the dam was mined and all the rest of the things you said. But Hajrudin Mesic and his people, they're not the ones we handed this over to. The local president of the local community and some other man holding another post, that's who those pistols were handed over to, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the dam had been blown up, what damage would it have caused?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been a terrible ecological disaster. The silt would flow into the river. That was not the aim. They realised what would happen. Maybe some people were not aware of the grave danger, but they took up positions precisely to protect that dam. I'm not an expert for these things, and I can't claim anything. I just know that the acids are very dangerous, and these would probably provoke an ecological disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that in this same period of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, with the permission of the Chamber I'd just like to ask you a couple of points for clarification. Very briefly, my learned friend has raised quite a number of points about the alleged mining of this dam. Now, can you kindly tell the Chamber whether this alleged mining took place before or after Zvornik had been attacked by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side had already attacked Zvornik and taken control of it. Zvornik had been taken control of by paramilitary units and the army of Republika Srpska and the active troops from Serbia. They had already captured Zvornik and looted it, and the population had already moved out. So this happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And was the dam, in the event, blown up?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Nor did they have anything to blow it up with. Where would it come from? We had handed over all our weapons. How could we blow it up? We were promised safety if we handed in our weapons. The weapons were surrendered, and afterwards they told us that we would be exchanged, and then what happened, happened; only four or five people survived this exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I just now want to bring you back to the Karakaj Technical School where you say that you were detained. Now, in your statement, you say that 50 to 80 or maybe a hundred people were seen by you dead there. Who was guarding this facility?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the formation, nor did it ever occur to me to ask. You didn't dare ask. I don't know what that unit was called or who they were, those men. There were locals, there were others; now, how the formation was called, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: But in your view, it would have been this formation that would have been responsible for the people who died in the technical school?

utterances.speaker: Witness B-1097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They were responsible. You can imagine there were about 1.000 men in a small area, and they would turn on the heating. And I don't know how many people died, but -- I didn't count them, but up to 80 were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No further questions, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Witness B-1097, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. Thank you for coming back. I'm sorry you had to make two journeys, but your evidence is now over, and you're free to go, but would you just wait until the blinds are turned down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and it was an honour for me to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We could make a start with the blinds down, although they will be turned up in a moment. There were various administrative matters you wanted to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only a few but they're designed to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might it be convenient to take them now rather than at the end of the session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber is, of course, aware that there is our final application of the 21st of October to add further witnesses. There's been a corrigendum to that which has been filed. I don't know if the Chamber is going to want it any more rapidly than coming through Registry in the normal way, and I have to say that I'm grateful for having been alerted to one of the needs to correct the earlier document by a member of the Court staff who spotted an error that we had, I'm afraid, let slip through, for which, of course, I take full responsibility. We've now received the motion from the amicus, and I had to some degree already forecast or acted in anticipation of their response, because it seemed to me that we should recognise the realities of the time constraints we're under, and although there was once a time when it looked as though we would be able to get very nearly all our witnesses in, we were down to a margin of about five days, that margin has grown over recent weeks because of the time that has been taken, principally in cross-examination, and it's therefore appropriate that I should alert the Chamber, the accused, and the amici to the witnesses whom we realistically hope to be able to fit into the available time, thus to identify those who we do not expect to be able to fit into the available time. There are now a sufficiently limited number of weeks left before the end of our case that we can move, I think, in order to help you from the chart that we've become familiar with, which has an arithmetical way of calculating whether we can get the witnesses in or not, to a chart that really - it will be with you tomorrow - simply sets out exactly the remaining days by date and day of the week and identifies, so far as we can, which witnesses we want to take on any particular day. That chart should be -- it's pretty well complete now but I want to finish the 92 bis witnesses we have yet to deal with and from whom we will be making certain deletions. That chart will be with you, at the latest, tomorrow morning. So I hope that will meet the it seemed to me understandable request of the amici to have more detail of the witnesses who it is likely to be called and meets what they were going to ask to be dealt with in 48 hours on a voluntary basis. The Chamber will recall that we are under an order to list exhibits. For the time being, I'm going to list exhibits within the 21 day allowed -- 21 days allowed for all witnesses on our list because although of course this is what we hope to be able to fit into the remaining few weeks of our case, unforeseen events can lead to witnesses not being available and, therefore, if they have to be substituted by other witnesses, we would of course give notice that we would seek to call those other witnesses from the list, but it's important that their exhibits are already notified. It may also be the case that there are exhibits from witnesses we -- or exhibits linked to particular witnesses who we won't have time to call but we'll nevertheless think are sufficiently important that they should go in through other witnesses. The list that you will have tomorrow has been prepared on the basis of the final application to add witnesses, i.e., it's been prepared on the basis of all witnesses we would wish to call. We recognise that we don't have yet any ruling on that, but that's the basis upon which we've done it. And the list of witnesses to be prepared and indeed of witnesses who -- for whom there will not be time probably to call includes, as it were, selections from both the old list and the additions. So it covers all of that. Can I, with that very brief explanation of where we are and how I'm hoping to help and map out the way to the end of the case, make a couple of points, I hope without incurring the Court's displeasure in any way. In the three-day week that we are now working, and with focused preparation, with the ability to use written witness statements in the way that we now are, it is possible for examination-in-chief, of course, to be conducted very short, very swiftly indeed. The Court may also think that in the same three-day week, with the accused now very well experienced in the common law skill of cross-examination, he can explore the heart of his case in cross-examination swiftly as well. And the third point I would make, general point, is the Court may have thought that the experience with Lord Owen as a witness showed the advantages in several ways of some types of witnesses. He would be perhaps one, coming to court without any preparation and yet being dealt with, I hope, succinctly and efficiently, a couple of hours by us, and it would be our submission the heart of the cross-examination similarly actually dealt with, drawn from that witness in a couple of hours. And I mention that because the chart will show the Chamber tomorrow morning just how tight things are for us to get in evidence that you will see and you'll see why we think to be particularly important. And with this chart in mind, the Chamber may want to have in mind that there will be several witnesses, important witnesses, who it looks as though we simply won't have time to call. Now, the Chamber may want to have some of those in mind as possible people we can't call. Perhaps I can go into private session just for a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are some high-level witnesses in the schedule that will come tomorrow, perhaps not unlike Lord Owen and General Naumann and people like that in the most general terms, who thus far have typically taken part of the second day at least. The Chamber will see from the schedule when it's available that these witnesses, if they do take that sort of period of time, are likely simply to knock out our possibility of calling other witnesses -- and I've made the point before of necessity, and I make no complaint of this, it's a matter ultimately of course for the Chamber -- if such witnesses take longer, then we may have to make the decision against calling some of them at all because of the knock-on effect they have. And so my request to the Chamber is perhaps if it has the time to think about this as a problem, to consider giving very strict timetables limited for all sides on some of these witnesses, bearing in mind that which I say is clear, namely that focused examination-in-chief and cross-examination can in fact draw the heart of the evidence of these witnesses in a short period of time. Three last time-sensitive witness issues that I'd be grateful for the Chamber and my learned friends and indeed the accused to consider as follows, advanced notice really: Witness 110 is a witness who it is suggested in your witness list is not a witness at all. It's a person who could produce the commission of experts report, schedule 6, which deals with Sarajevo. The whole issue of the commission of experts report is one we ought to address at some stage. It may be a self-propelling document. It may not be a document acceptable to the Chamber, but I would be grateful for an opportunity a little later to discuss it. Witness 141 is an in-house witness we've identified as somebody who could assist with interpretation of intercepts and possibly other documents of the type that we know are still being considered in dealings with Serbia and Montenegro, if interpretation is necessary. My time-sensitive concern about this witness is as follows: If the proposition underlying calling such a witness is that interpretation of documents is appropriate in general, then cross-examination of such a witness would be very hard to limit, and I would be very anxious before calling such a witness for there to be an understanding of the limitations upon both examination-in-chief and cross-examination in order that it simply doesn't do damage to the very tight timetable. And my suggestion at this stage is that if such a witness is appropriate, and for intercepts such a witness is probably essential, we should tabulate the interpretive evidence that the witness would give and that cross-examination should be limited to that or to something very closely linked to that so as not to be too extensive. And finally, Witness 146 is the witness who can produce either the tapes or the transcripts of The Death of Yugoslavia and The Fall of Milosevic television programmes. The Chamber will recall that there were several interviews longer than those which were broadcast which will be available. I would hope that they can be accepted as evidence without any time being taken in court because they are essentially just written records, and I'd like to be able to address you about that in due course but I give notice that that's my position now. So, Your Honour, thank you for the time. The chart tomorrow first thing will set out a plan to the end of the case subject to the inevitable variations of witness availability, and at some stage I'd be grateful for the opportunity to consider those other few issues I've raised with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The next witness, there's a matter in private session I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber is going to adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Good morning or, rather, good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have been granted protective measures by the Court, image distortion and you have been assigned a pseudonym, B-1399. So I would like you to look at the piece of paper in front of you and tell us whether that's your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would offer his statement and the related exhibit as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have them at the moment. It may be they're just there to the right. Yes. If we could have those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number is 583, tab 1 to be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If the pseudonym sheet also could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number is 584, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll read out a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim born in Kamenica, in the Zvornik municipality. He was in Belgrade for 18 years and returned to Bosnia. On 13 March 1993 he moved to Srebrenica. After the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July, the witness decided with many other people, about 10 to 15.000 men, to go through the woods towards Tuzla. He decided to go through the woods because he feared that they would be killed when they would go to the UN base at Potocari. In the beginning of that journey, around the second day, the Muslims responded to loudspeakers and surrendered to the Serbs. The surrendering place was close to the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje, and they were received by about 50 Serb soldiers. They were ordered by the Serbs to sit down and hand over any money and personal belongings. There were about 2.000 to 2.500 people sitting on the meadow together at Sandici. The witness was alerted that troops from Arkan's men would be coming. They were also told to lie down and put their -- on their stomachs, and they had to shout, "Long live the King." Around half past seven in the evening, Mladic arrived at the meadow and told the people, the Muslim men, that they would be exchanged. Some women and children were allowed to go away from Sandici meadow towards Tuzla. After Mladic's speech, the Serbs ordered the men to board buses and trucks, and they were taken into the direction of Bratunac, where they eventually arrived around half past nine in the evening. Throughout the night, the witness had to spend the night together with his fellow people on the trucks. Serb soldiers came and asked specific people, Muslim men, from villages around Srebrenica out. They were taken to a nearby garage. The men in the vehicles could hear thuds and screaming and fire from automatic weapons, and then everything would go quiet. In the morning, the witness and all the other people on the vehicles were taken to Zvornik in a large convoy of about 30 vehicles. Eventually, the vehicles arrived at a schoolyard in Grbovci, close to Zvornik. There were about 30 soldiers outside the school. The gym where the witness entered was almost -- was already filled with about 700 to 800 people, some of them from Potocari. At the end, there were about 2.000 people in that gym and it was very hot. When the Muslim men would address the guards as soldiers, they would answer, "We are not soldiers. We are Karadzic's young Chetniks." At one point two soldiers and one Serb woman brought a pile of rags to blindfold the men. The witness was then forced, with about 30 other people, into a Tamic truck. The registration plates, the witness says, were either police or military in Cyrillic. The witness was brought in the truck to a very nearby location, was ordered out, lined up, and the firing started. One of the men fell on the witness and covered him. The witness himself, he was not hit. When one of the injured men begged, "Finish me off," a Serb soldier said, "Slowly, slowly." Later a Serb came and fired single shots at people. The witness assumed they were moving. Another truck came and the witness again heard shots. At this point the witness was still blindfolded and lying on his stomach. Trucks kept arriving and the gunfire continued late into the night. The witness also heard machinery around, an excavator and a loader. He also heard the Serbs talking to each other, calling each other by names. He specifically recognised the voice of a Gojko Simic who was the leader of that group, and this Gojko Simic told his people to go to a different location nearby and said, "Let's go to the meadow and kill the men." At one time in the evening, another person who survived jumped up and tried to escape. He caught the attention of the Serbs, and the witness himself used that moment and himself stood up and escaped, crawling out from the bodies. He followed a nearby railway track to a railway station, returned back again to the location where the executions took place. Now he saw from a distance of about 20 metres in the moonlight a lot of bodies and clothes. After about ten days of walking, the witness made it into the free territory. This concludes the summary, Mr. President, and I do have a few additional questions. It shouldn't take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, we heard that you were in Belgrade for some time, in fact 18 years. Now, when you came back, to which village did you come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: The village of Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was there a time when you left this village again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I left at the end of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you left this village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Because we were forced out by the Serb forces, the army from Republika Srpska with the help of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what the population was of this village? Was it inhabited --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Between 5 and 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were they Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Mostly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where did you flee to from Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: We fled towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you leave Konjevic Polje at one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, we did. When General Morillon arrived with the APCs. Then an order reached us from somebody who had been negotiating with him that we were to move towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we heard that you were at a gym in Grbovci and that there were about 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember a specific soldier who had a beret wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A soldier did have a red beret with a cross and the sign of the four Ss in Cyrillic, and that's when they started taking people off to be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he follow the people who were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, probably because when the truck was full, it would be empty when it returned while I was in the hall, before I'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Two questions to finish: Why did you leave Srebrenica? Why did you decide to go through the woods rather than to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, because we were afraid of retaliation from the Serbs, because the Serbs retaliated everywhere without exception. Not only Srebrenica but everywhere else. They didn't spare any civilian or military-able man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question would be: Do you remember giving a witness statement to the MUP in Tuzla on 1st of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember saying that you were surrendering at Sandici on the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. We surrendered on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I have one additional point to mention, and we should go private. Just a reminder to everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be switched on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, up until April 1992, you lived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which means for almost two decades; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, not two decades. I as a worker lived there, but my family stayed on in my native village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how long did you live in Belgrade as a worker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: About 15 years, but my company was from Belgrade, and I first found employment in Cacak and the head office was in Belgrade, and I think I arrived in 1987 in Belgrade and found a job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that after a series of years spent working in Belgrade, when the war broke out you went to Kamenica, which is the Zvornik municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, while you were living and working in Belgrade, did you ever feel you had any problems because of the fact that you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. I had no problems then at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from -- you left Belgrade because the war started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. It was our Bajram holiday. The Bajram holiday was on the Saturday, the 4th of April, and we left Belgrade on the 3rd of April, and at the Ruma crossroads, one bus was returned back to Belgrade. We started off a little later, but they turned us back from Soca, and afterwards we took the Obrenovac road. When we were in Obrenovac we were stopped by the Serb police. There were just three policemen. One of them was in a container and two of them had automatic rifles on them, and we were told to wait while the one in the container called up Avala 6. And I assume you know who Avala 6 was, better than me. I don't know who it was, but they told the driver and the man sitting next to the driver who was a representative because it was a privately owned coach, he said come over here, take lists of passengers in the bus with you. And our driver left. He was a private entrepreneur from Zemun, and when he came back he said they won't allow us safe passage, they won't allow us to go through. And the bus was stopped. However, the passengers asked that we carry our journey on foot because we thought if they won't let the buses through perhaps we could go through on foot. The policeman from the container called up again and then they allowed us to pass through and we didn't have any more problems until we reached home. After that, the war broke out in Zvornik. Zvornik fell on the 7th of April and I wasn't able to go back to Belgrade after that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. So were you not a witness for the other side, you would be proof and evidence of the fact that the people from Serbia or, rather, those living in Serbia during the war went to Bosnia. So that I assume is proof of Serbia's aggression against Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying you lived in Belgrade and then you were able to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I lived in Belgrade, but my family members were always in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1399. Now, were you in your village when at the beginning of April 1992, without any reason whatsoever, five Serb young men were arrested precisely in your village, the village of Kamenica, and they were interrogated by a policeman from the village by the name of Avdija Omerovic. And in view of the fact that this incident triggered off great unrest amongst the Serb population in the municipality, do you happen to recall the event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Avdija Omerovic was not a policeman in Kamenica and those five Serb young men were never taken prisoner in Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, excellent. So we can move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that at the time the paramilitary unit in Zvornik and the surrounding parts were organised in the form of a reserve composition of the police force itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. Kamenica remained under siege in an encirclement. We had no contacts with Zvornik after the 5th or 6th of April. We had no contacts with Zvornik at all. It was just our village and the surrounding villages in the direction of Sarajevo that were encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, is it true that the conflicts in your region started on the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. On the 26th of April, we were first attacked by the army because a Serb came and told the Muslims of Sekovic, he said, Brethren Muslims -- people say he actually cried. I don't know the man very well. I know his name but I don't want to give it. He said, flee, run, because there's the army in Pavlovic with some tanks, and those tanks actually did attack us after that. That's what he said to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, do you happen to remember that the Mosque Doves and the other Muslim formations acted from fulcrums at Kamenica, points of support and strongholds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. I heard about that in Tuzla. I heard about this dove unit, but there weren't any men from that unit where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you have then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: We just had the TO, because we had to defend ourselves if anybody attacked us, but we didn't have the means to defend ourselves with. We didn't have a BH army, and the army had to be formed in the course of the war, and it was all on our backs and through the people that had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you called it the Territorial Defence, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that at the time, regardless of what these units of yours were called, that you would attack the suburbs of Zvornik during the night? You would topple Serb houses, burn them, loot them, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. None of us dared go to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Zvornik, I'm talking about the environs of Zvornik. Do you remember that on the 24th of August, for example, 1992, you attacked the village of Gornje Kamenica in the Zvornik municipality and on the occasion you set fire to all the houses, you desecrated the Orthodox cemetery in the village, destroyed all the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb village, Mr. Milosevic, was attacked when they provoked us too much. We had no way out other than to do that. Now, you're saying all this, whereas how many Muslim houses after the fall in 1992 were mined and blown up, including two Serb houses? Kukoj Velja's [phoen] house and Velja Tomic's house. They were neighbouring houses and I think that Tomic Velja's wife is now prosecuting the army for having destroyed her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, all right. Is it true that your particular unit at that time attacked Gornje Kamenica and that in the attack a number of Serbs were killed, Serb houses set fire to, destroyed, and looted? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know whether they killed anyone or not, but I do know that this operation did take place. Now, what actually happened I can't say, but we never heard of any civilians being killed. Perhaps some soldiers were, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember for example Ljubomir Tomic, Dragomir Tomic, civilians and others who were killed during that attack, other Serbs skilled in Gornje Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: They were not civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This man Velimir Tomic, he wanted to strangle a woman when he raised the Serb flag on the mosque, on the minaret of the mosque. And I can give the woman's name. She was a Muslim woman. She took down the flag because she said it's -- there's -- it's not the right place for that flag. You take the flag to its rightful place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this other man that was killed, was that the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. I don't know when any of these people were killed, either of them. I don't know when they were killed. But this man, Velimir Tomic was not a civilian. He was a military man, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Ljubomir Tomic and Dragomir Tomic, not Velimir Tomic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: There is no Ljubomir Tomic as far as I know Kamenica. There's nobody by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know all the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, I do because it's a small village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many Serbs were killed in that small village, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't say. I'm just saying that I've heard of a man called Velimir Tomic and that he was killed, but I haven't heard of a Ljubomir Tomic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, why did your forces attack this small Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, it's not a small village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've just said it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, it's not a small village. You said small village. Those Serb forces killed our own people, and people had had it -- had as much as they could take. You don't know our region. You had the artillery. The Serbs had artillery. We didn't even have rifles. And if we had a few bullets we just had a few bullets in our hands. Nobody gave the Bosnian Muslims, our army, any ammunition and tanks. You gave tanks to the Serbs. They had aeroplanes, they had everything; we had nothing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1399. Well, what did you use to kill all those Serbs with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, just rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So rifles. Is that a mitigating circumstance, killing them with rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Don't say me. I didn't kill anybody. You're saying "you." I didn't kill anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, please: Do you remember the conflict that took place on the 5th of November, 1992, precisely in the Kamenica area when your forces captured and then killed a large number of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: They did not capture them. Whether they killed them, I don't know. I saw several dead Serbs but they didn't capture them anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't first capture them and then kill them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many Serbs did they kill on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I saw several Serbs, and they were all soldiers wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it true and correct that the defenders of the Serbian village of Kamenica were forced to withdraw precisely in the face of your attack, your onslaught, and that afterwards, the ones who were captured were killed in the most brutal way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, that's not true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that when the bodies were uncovered, some of the bodies had their heads severed, or armed or legs, and they were mutilated bodies cut into pieces? There is documentation about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: That's just fabrication. I don't believe any of that happened anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of the bodies had chains on them. They had been tied. Some had holes made with nails and poles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know about any of that. I guarantee that never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since a moment ago you said that you knew all those people over there who were living there, I have here some information that the bodies of Uros Kozanovic [phoen], Radislav Grabovic, his body had one leg and one arm missing. Vlado Grabovic, a beheaded body. Jokic Savo, also he was beheaded and there was a chain on one of his legs. Radoslav Matsanovic [phoen], who was slaughtered. Radomir Pavlovic with his head cut off, Miladin Asteris [phoen] was in a state of decomposition. Vladimir Bozic, his body was mutilated and his head cut off, and his skull broken apart with a blunt object. Slavko Tijanic, a head without eyes, ears, or nose, and crushed, and in his chest there was a 6-millimetre pole.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, don't make those things up. That didn't happen. Only the Serbs could have done that. No one else. Don't waste your time with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb and I'm telling you these things. You're claiming it's not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those people were not killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: They may have been killed but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to make much progress with this. Mr. Milosevic, these are a series of allegations that you're making, a series of allegations. The witness knows nothing about them. In due course, you will have the opportunity, as you've been told often enough, to call your own witness. Meanwhile, let us move on to something which the witness can deal with. You've heard the evidence which he's given.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Mr. May. He has testified about where he was all that time, and he also testified that the army that he calls the Territorial Defence carried out an attack which he himself mentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me please, Mr. 1399, do you know a single one of the names that I have listed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, not one of them. Not one of them is an inhabitant of Kamenica. You can check that out through people who really know the people from Kamenica. There are no such surnames in Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not a single one of these persons was killed in Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a waste of time arguing with him. He's told you he knows nothing about what you're talking about. No point going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these names that I have read out, do you know the name of Radan Pavlovic, Savo Kazanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're wasting your time. Let's move on to something else. I don't know what the purpose of this cross-examination is at all. You've heard what this witness has told the Court. You've heard his evidence. You're not challenging that at all, simply trying to put up some sort of counter-case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to that too, Mr. May, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you familiar with the name Muhamed Ibrahimbegovic from Kamenica -- Kemal Ibrahimbegovic from Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they in command of units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, not one of them were in command. They were drivers in Drinatrans. Both of those men I don't believe ever took a rifle into their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please, when did you go to Srebrenica? Was it at the time a protected area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: When we arrived in Srebrenica, Srebrenica was supposed to be proclaimed a safe area. The Canadian Battalion came a couple of days later. I don't think it was at that moment, but shortly afterwards it was proclaimed a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when did you go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: On the 13th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who were the commanders of the Muslim forces in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know who were the commanders. Everyone knows that there was Naser Oric as the previous commander, and when it became a demilitarised zone, there were no commanders. Who would be the commander then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the crimes committed from Srebrenica in that area, in the surrounding area, in the villages? You know the village of Gniona, Bijeceva, Skelani, Ciceva, Vigora --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant, Mr. May, because it was from this safe area, from Srebrenica, that the most horrific crimes were committed against the Serbs. I have a half a page listing just the names of the villages that were attacked from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that in relation to the crimes committed at Srebrenica and the massacre that took place there? Are you saying that somehow what happened was justified or are you saying it is an excuse of some sort? Otherwise, it doesn't seem to have any relevance at all. The fact that the other side may have committed crimes is totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, not a single crime can be justified by another crime. I'm just speaking of the need for us to see the context within which this was happening, the circumstances under which these events took place, and the terrible suffering that happened in the area and which was characteristic of all those years which involve great suffering of the people in the area. And of course, one crime does not justify another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the point, and this is a very central point in the trial. Whether there were or were not other crimes is really beside the point. The central matter we're dealing with are the crimes alleged in the indictment, and at the moment, the context does not appear to have any particular relevance as far as the commission of the crimes are concerned. It may -- if it were true, it may explain why the crimes were committed. It may provide, if it's said, provocation, but that of course is no defence at all.
