You should understand that, and there is a limit to the amount of time that we can spend upon these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I truly have nothing to defend myself against here. What I'm trying to do is to establish the truth, and I really have nothing to defend myself against when it comes to the crime in Srebrenica or anything else, because Serbia and I personally struggled to achieve peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't you, Mr. Milosevic, say that. You kept saying throughout the war you Serbs should be in one state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us avoid -- no, if you wouldn't mind. Let us avoid a free-for-all. Mr. Milosevic, I'm not going to stop you specifically asking these questions, but you ought to bear in mind that they are of peripheral relevance at best. Your case appears to be that what happened at Srebrenica was nothing to do with you. That's what you seem to be saying. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can't seem to be. I believe you know full well that what happened in Srebrenica has nothing to do with Serbia or me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, is it true that all the Serb villages except for the immediate vicinity of Bratunac and Skelani were burnt and destroyed and razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: When I came to Srebrenica, the villages had been left by the Serbs. Who chased them out, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: They either went on their own or I don't know what. I arrived in 1993 when it was to become a safe area. There was no fighting around Srebrenica at that time when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that out of 52 settlements of Srebrenica municipality inhabited by Serbs there were Serbs only in Srbica, Jaska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're just wasting time with these questions. Now, move on to something else that the witness can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to time, we would suggest that if the accused doesn't put relevant questions to this witness in relation to what his evidence is, that this witness would be free to go after today and doesn't need to stay overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be a matter for us to determine. Is there any particular reason why he has to go today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Mr. President. It's merely the rest of the timetable. We have, as you know, more witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you lived in the safe area of Srebrenica for a time, do you remember that the 8th Operative Group, which was later renamed the 28th division, was actually formed and enlarged in that very safe area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. The 28th Division was formed when the people who survived reached free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please, is it true, and I will respect the requirement to ask you certain things in private session, but I will refer to what is known as the statement, that your brother was a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member, but he was only a cook. Because you know when a zone is demilitarised, no one can carry weapons except UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, are you claiming that Srebrenica was the demilitarised zone and that there wasn't a strong Muslim formation in Srebrenica, people who were carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Only UNPROFOR. No one could carry weapons. If they were to be seen by UNPROFOR, the weapons would be seized from him. That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the numerical strength of the people under weapons in Srebrenica was 10.913 fighters as of the 1st of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Who could say that with accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the numerical strength?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: When we headed towards Tuzla, there may have been 200 or 300, maybe 500, but not 10.000. We didn't have 10.000 pieces of weapons even if we hadn't surrendered them to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this figure is not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that this 28th Infantry Division consisted of five brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many brigades it had. I just know that when we reached free territory - I don't know which month it was when the 28th brigade was formed. It consisted of the men who were in Tuzla who had left before, who hadn't gone to Srebrenica but had gone from Kamenica and other villages to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's another matter, Tuzla. Is it true that in July 1995 when these events in Srebrenica occurred, there were between 12 and 13.000 combatants in the Muslim forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't think there were that many able-bodied men. As for weapons, never did one in five have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall that on the 21st of January, 1995, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina introduced restrictions on the freedom of movement of the UN in the area known -- the triangular area known as Bandera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They held at the time about 100 soldiers of the Dutch Battalion as hostages from the 27th to the 31st of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: That never happened, I guarantee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that before these events in Srebrenica the army of Republika Srpska was only responding to attacks by the BH army coming from that safe area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't even bother to consider it. It's not for the witness to answer that sort of question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all? Were you in a military unit when you were in Srebrenica or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that offensive sabotage operations were launched from Srebrenica in territories outside the safe area inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I wasn't a member of the army, and if anyone did that, it wouldn't be known. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it shouldn't be known, but it was covered up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, so I can't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to the number of people who were killed at the time as a result of these operations launched from the safe area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the surroundings, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I'm telling you, in 1993 when I arrived, it was a demilitarised zone. So I don't know anything about the situation before that. If somebody did conduct any act of sabotage, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1399. So you're claiming that Srebrenica was demilitarised, that the Muslims in Srebrenica didn't have weapons, and that there was no combat there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that there are many documents showing that there was no respect of the safe area principles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Maybe the Serbs didn't respect it, but we had to respect it because our weapons were seized from us. You were the ones who didn't respect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, please don't speak in the second person plural.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: The Serbs wouldn't do anything without Serbia. That's beyond question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, there's a document, a letter from April 1995 whereby Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, the commander of the Dutch Battalion, writes to Osman Suljic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to pay attention to what the Prosecution suggest. If you do not ask this witness relevant questions, questions which he can answer, not questions about the commander of the Dutch Battalion -- he is not here to give that sort of evidence. He's giving evidence about what he saw and heard himself. Unless he's asked relevant questions, then your cross-examination will have to be brought to an end. Now, if you've got any relevant questions for him, now is your chance to ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what is called your statement, one can see that you saw quite a number of men with arms after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I saw about 200, 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw them with your own eyes, 200 or 300 men under arms of the Muslim forces after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge regarding the internal inter-Muslim conflicts, rebellions, lootings, clashes between the civilian and military structures, attacks on UN members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, no. There may have been some minor incidents, some minor clashes. Nobody knew about them anyway, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a battle against these disbanded force -- Muslim forces after the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: What disbanded forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say 200, 300, and so on. Hundreds of men who were armed and who you saw after the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: When we left Srebrenica, when we were leaving Srebrenica, I don't know, I was in the last column on the 12th. Maybe 4.00 or half past four we left the territory of Srebrenica. I don't know where those men with weapons were, whether there were any ambushes anywhere. I didn't know anything about that. It was a large column, there were lots of people. Some were ten kilometres ahead. So I didn't know at all what was going on. When we were captured, we were surrounded. The Serbs asked us to surrender, they guaranteed our safety, and you know what happened when we surrendered, you know what happened to us. Everyone knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, just tell me, please: Was there fighting when you were breaking through the encirclement, that is, the armed formations when they were leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I wasn't involved. The people had to get out because the Serb army would not allow them to leave in a negotiated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you recollect how long prior to these events in Srebrenica had Naser Oric and a large group of commanders and leaders leave Srebrenica? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that after Srebrenica was captured, do you know anything about measures taken by the army of Republika Srpska? I'm not talking about the group that carried out the executions. I'm talking about the army of Republika Srpska. Did it undertake any measures to ensure the evacuation of all those who wished to leave and to assist in the removal of the civilians from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: As far as civilians are concerned, the civilians were seen off, but they separated a large number of men, elderly people, and middle-aged men, because one of my brothers, thanks to some good luck, his leg hurt him. He wasn't wounded. He had to carry two crutches, and he was released. And he said that Serbs were separated, and I just happened to be lucky. A soldier told me to get on the truck and I said I can't climb on, my leg hurts. And he said, Can you get on a bus? And I said I could, he showed me the bus. And that is how he crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, 1399. I want to make one thing clear: There is no question regarding condemnation of the crime in Srebrenica. I just wish to separate what is obvious; that is, did the official army of Republika Srpska in those days protect the civilian population and provide for their evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes. The women and children and some elderly. But all the others, older and younger ones, were taken away. And wherever there were executions, this mass genocide that was committed involved the elderly as well as younger people from the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the information I have - please confirm or deny them - some sort of an agreement was reached and signed by representatives of Srebrenica on their behalf, a certain Nasib Mandzic, a civilian representative of Republika Srpska, and the commander of the Dutch Battalion regarding the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: They may have. I'm not guaranteeing that they didn't, but the Serbs did not respect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a representative of the Dutch Battalion later signed a statement saying that the evacuation had been carried out in accordance with the plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why were the Dutch Battalion not allowed to make statements for four days? And in those four days the genocide was committed. That was my question. That was the question addressed to the Dutch generals by representatives of the BH, especially by a Serb general who remained in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to check out certain facts that I was able to get hold of, because I care very much about those events in Srebrenica being fully discovered and revealed and for those responsible to answer for it and not those who are not. So I'm not asking you about the document, as you were not in a position to know about documents, but there are documents, and I'm asking you of your knowledge. I also have the number and everything else, 19th of July, 1995, where it says that the commander of the Drina Corps unit were cooperating with UNPROFOR to protect the Muslim population to guarantee their security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This witness can't deal with Drina Corps documents. He had nothing to do with that at all. You could call the appropriate witness to deal with it in due course, but it's no good asking this witness, who was a survivor of what happened, of the detailed documents there may have been.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May, but I would like to separate the behaviour of the regular forces of Republika Srpska from the behaviour of these groups who perpetrated the crimes, because it is very important to find out who perpetrated those crimes and who stands behind them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You would perhaps ask him about the men he saw. Perhaps ask him about that and to describe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Ratko Mladic personally ordered the medical evacuation from Bratunac so that the wounded, the elderly, the sick should be evacuated in a safe manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Some of the wounded reached free territory, some didn't. There was a man with me who had a wooden leg. A shell took away about 2 centimetres of his foot. All the wounded were not protected. Some were; some were not. When he was just about to reach free territory, he was killed. One person -- some women saw that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Left me ask you, I have here the text of an original article from Slobodna Bosna dated the 14th of July, 1996. Ibrahim Mustafic, a Republican and federal deputy founder and former president of the SDA in Srebrenica and the captain of the Serbian army after the fall of the city. He speaks about the events there, so I'm just asking you is what he said true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'll read it out to you and then you'll tell me whether that concurs with your own knowledge. He was asked: "Who were the people that you are accusing and who you no longer trust? "Mustafic: The scenario for the betrayal of Srebrenica was consciously prepared. Unfortunately, the Presidency of BH was directly involved in this as well as the General Staff. If you want the names, you know who those people are. I understood the situation in Srebrenica, and rest assured that there would be far many people of Srebrenica alive if a group of Mafioso did not oppose me. If I had been told to fire from the demilitarised zone, I would not have obeyed that order, because I would tell those people who had their wives and children there to do it." And then they ask him: "What were the consequences of operations from the demilitarised zone?" Mustafa said: "It was conscious, giving justification to the Serbian forces to attack the demilitarised zone." And then he goes on to say that through some people who were close to the Croatian intelligence and who have contacts with the Serbs, he had heard that there were another 5.600 living people from Srebrenica and Miss Maholica Tomalica [phoen] told me recently that she had some information from the human rights committee that there were 4.500 such people, et cetera. Was it ever established in these regular proceedings engaged in by the army of Republika Srpska, that is to evacuate and to protect the population, how many people were evacuated and protected and how many were killed in all in those crimes committed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I think about 7.000 or 8.000 people were killed. I don't know how many were evacuated. Women, children, and men. I know until the command came to separate the men, men passed through and some younger men could pass. And when they started separating, they separated all the men, and they didn't hurt children under 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1399. That prisoners of war were separated, that is one thing. Now, tell me, who, to the best of your knowledge, committed that crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: The Serbs. The army of Republika Srpska with the assistance of paramilitary units or the JNA. And anyway, the JNA was just the same as the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have nothing more precise to say regarding your knowledge as to who committed those crimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I'm telling you, when the crime was about to be committed, when we were detained, some soldiers came, and they first lined up the people, the elderly people who were at the other end of the hall. They had to get up on their feet. The order was about turn to the right and to turn their back to the door. And when they were taking people out and blindfolding them, they told the others to turn their back to the door so that they wouldn't see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1399, that was not my question. You said just now in this brief examination-in-chief, and I noted it down, that there were 2.000 people in the hall at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, not in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He said -- he said specifically they didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume I'm quoting you correctly when I say that you said that some armed people turned up and that they said they were not soldiers but some young Chetniks. That's how they introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No, they were the soldiers who were on duty at the door while we were in the hall. They were very young guys, and if anybody were to address them by saying, "Comrade Solider," they would say, "We're not soldiers, we're Karadzic's Chetniks without a beard."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what they said about themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said about themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, were those the people that carried out the executions or not, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. Those people stayed where they were. Other people probably carried out those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you have any knowledge as to who those others were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, there was a colleague of mine who worked in Belgrade. We've known each other for 15 to 18 years, Gojko Simic. He's my own age, from that village around Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is he one the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes, and he was one of the main ones, the chief ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many other perpetrators were with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Well, I would say there were at least six or seven people, because where I was, where the execution took place and where there was no more room, this man Simic Gojko said, now, let anybody of those people that they thought were killed speak up. Gojko, Vojo, Risto. They called out to those people. And when they were supposed to leave, the man digging the pit with the excavator stopped the excavator and told him, "If you all leave I'll switch the engine off and I'll leave too."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just try to be more efficient. When you surrendered on the road at Sandici you saw a young man who said you were going to be exchanged; is that right? You saw Mladic who said you were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no other mistreatment of your suffering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: No. Mladic didn't say that we would suffer. He just said we would go to some hangars and be given water, although not dinner, but the other man said we would be getting dinner too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was mention of some regular type of exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you mention the school in Grbovci, that that's where they took you, and then took you to the execution site.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say your eyes were tied.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how were you able to see corpses along the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Not along the way. We didn't see them along the way. When they lined us up for execution, I was looking down, looking down in front of myself and all you could do was see underneath you. I happened to see a dead man. Otherwise, when we were going along in the truck under tarpaulin, you weren't able to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that they -- there was a burst of gunfire. At what distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know, my eyes were tied. Probably they shot at our backs. How far away, one or two metres they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, all right. You say yourself that this group of people that perpetrated the crime, the crime we're discussing, numbered six or seven men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any knowledge whatsoever as to who that group of men were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know that Gojko Simic was there. Vojo, Risto. I don't know the others except for Gojko Simic. One of them was called by nickname but when they went to another location and this man with the excavator didn't want to stay, then this man Gojko left three soldiers there and said let's go to the meadow to kill the people, and they went down there and that's when the shooting started, while the people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those six -- you said six men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: Six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, six or seven men. Did anybody else take part in that execution, the one that you survived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1399
utterances.text: I don't know. How should I know? All I know is that when they gathered together there and when Gojko left with that group of men, that three men stayed on, which means three or four others could have been there because one or two wouldn't have been enough to carry that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. You've got ten minutes left, Mr. Milosevic, for tomorrow. Witness 1399, we're going to adjourn now. Could you please come back tomorrow at 9.00 to complete your evidence, and could you also remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about it, about your evidence, that is, until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of November, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
